title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
abstract: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

title: Scale-Induced Semantic Shift in Visual Prompt Injection Against VLMs and Web Agents
abstract: Visual content in multimedia systems may be resized, compressed, or re-rendered before it is interpreted by a vision-language model. We study a security failure mode in which these transformations change the machine-readable semantics of an image: a textual instruction is not recovered at a $512\times512$ presentation resolution under our evaluation protocol but becomes recoverable after aggressive downsampling. We formulate this behavior as Scale-Induced Semantic Shift (SISS) and develop a closed-loop black-box framework that combines dual-scale verification, selective self-hardening, shallow-layer low-rank adaptation, and pixel-space noise regularization. On a fixed 300-case benchmark, the third SISS refinement round obtains a $58.75\%$ average attack success rate across four closed-source vision-language models, compared with $41.08\%$ for the strongest generation baseline. A controlled sweep bounds the effect to aggressive compression: average success decreases to $17.68\%$, $6.85\%$, and $5.60\%$ at $128\times128$, $224\times224$, and $336\times336$, respectively. In a downstream web-agent study, the generated images increase hidden-instruction perception, but absolute behavioral compromise remains about $4\%$. Generic input transformations provide little protection in a separate defense protocol, whereas the proposed ScaleGuard consistency detector reduces non-adaptive success from $61.4\%$ to $24.3\%$ and one-round defense-aware success from $42.5\%$ to $15.0\%$, with no observed rejection among matched clean controls. The results characterize a bounded but reproducible semantic inconsistency in multimedia preprocessing and motivate scale-consistent visual-language inference.

title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents
abstract: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. Across all evaluations, Intent Profile-based protection outperforms all profile-free baselines on the primary metric. On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%). On more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajectories, where ground truth comes from environment state, profile-based post-execution detection reaches 0.949 AUROC versus AlignmentCheck 0.909, 0.897 with raw agent configuration and 0.843 without context. Profile-based input alignment improves protection success by 7 points over DataFilter with a comparable benign utility. These results suggest that an agent's intended purpose can serve as a useful security reference for detecting and mitigating deviations from its deployed role and operational boundaries.

title: Scaling public input on AI policy with pluralistic agents
abstract: AI is being deployed across a vast range of application domains, cultural environments, and human stakeholders. Safe and responsible AI development requires continuously accounting for diverse perspectives. We develop and test pluralistic agents, AI agent representatives that deliberate on behalf of individuals to align AI systems with diverse human perspectives. Pluralistic agents could help people contribute to many more discussions than they could directly participate in, on technical topics that would require training, and on policy choices that rely on private information that corporations and governments cannot readily share. Our experiments identify opportunities, risks, and perceptions of pluralistic agents. Agents were able to reliably shift policies in the direction of their represented persona's preferences, but the extent of each agent's influence was sensitive to the instructions from its persona, such as having more influence when instructed to be more verbose or less cooperative. This suggests that influence in AI-assisted deliberation could vary based on how participants prompt their agents and how the system is designed. In a preregistered study, 746 humans participated in the pluralistic agents process. Participants viewed pluralistic agents as useful and fair, preferring agents over the baseline of providing input to a single AI reasoning model. Most participants preferred participating themselves over either pluralistic agents or the baseline, but pluralistic agents recovered 68% of the baseline-direct gap in reported satisfaction and 82% in fairness. Because pluralistic agents can be used in many real-world contexts where direct discussion is not, they could be a promising tool to scale AI safety policy development. We encourage cautious exploration of this method, playing to its strengths as an amplifier of human input rather than a replacement.

title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as primary interfaces for factual retrieval, yet current evaluation paradigms rely almost exclusively on explicit entity names. In this work, we demonstrate that LLM knowledge is fundamentally lexically anchored: models possess extensive factual information but find it significantly difficult to retrieve without explicit name tokens. To quantify this limitation, we introduce ShadowBench, a rigorously hardened, shortcut-resistant benchmark designed to evaluate Latent Entity Association via a novel Dual-Trait Association (DTA) task. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive "Shadow Gap" across all model scales$\unicode{x2013}$up to the frontier models GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6$\unicode{x2013}$where removing lexical anchors causes performance drops of over 20%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this lexical dependency exposes a critical vulnerability in AI safety. Applying ShadowBench to Machine Unlearning, we find that state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., Gradient Difference, NPO) achieve only superficial lexical erasure. While unlearned models fail on direct queries, our novel Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) metric reveals that for popular entities, models explicitly reconstruct the "forgotten" entity in their internal reasoning traces in over 74% of cases, utilizing residual shadow knowledge to solve associative tasks. Conversely, for niche entities, models retain high shadow accuracy (60-90%) via implicit attribute correlation despite 0% LELR. Ultimately, ShadowBench indicates that current unlearning paradigms create an "Illusion of Forgetting," demonstrating that existing methods act as superficial output filters and are not yet reliable for achieving true parametric erasure.

title: Smart Model Routing for Order-of-Magnitude LLM Cost Reduction
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) deliver the strongest response quality but carry per-token prices often more than an order of magnitude above those of smaller, task-adequate models. Smart model routing addresses this mismatch by assigning each query to the cheapest model expected to answer it adequately, rather than sending every request to the most capable, most expensive endpoint. This paper develops a formal cost-quality optimization framework for routing -- including a derived optimal threshold-policy structure, a calibration-versus-discrimination distinction, a cascade breakeven condition, and a sensitivity analysis over price ratio and traffic skew -- situates that framework against the principal routing architectures and the signals used to estimate query difficulty, and works through a numerical example showing how a calibrated router can reduce blended inference cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an always-frontier deployment under specific, stated pricing and traffic assumptions, reporting both the gross reduction from routing policy alone and the net figure with the router's own overhead priced in. We situate this figure against the range reported by published routing systems (roughly 2x to frontier-level accuracy at one-fifth the cost), and close with the practical risks -- under- and over-routing, aggregate quality constraints masking segment-level harm, calibration without discrimination, calibration drift, prompt injection into routing signals, and operational failures such as tier outages and multi-provider price variation -- that determine whether the savings materialize in production. The analysis is primarily analytical, complemented by a GSM8K evaluation of the cascade framework (Section 5), validated (Section 5.2); extending the evaluation across tasks and model families is future work.

title: An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells
abstract: Understanding the persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety motivates an investigation of the dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry studied in singular learning theory. We analyze this persistence through transitions between singular wells. We establish an Eyring-Kramers formula for a low temperature Langevin diffusion between two compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. The wells may be singular and nonisolated, and the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle, with gates understood as inclusion-minimal sets meeting every minimizing path. A boundary-gate construction shows that uniqueness of this inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to every minimizing path passing through the saddle and one such path meeting the communication level only there. Compact semianalytic topology provides a separating function away from a fixed saddle neighborhood; analytic Morse coordinates give matching capacity bounds by first sending the temperature to zero and then shrinking that neighborhood. An anchored energy estimate and a small-ball potential-theoretic identity give uniformity for deterministic starting points. The leading constant is expressed in terms of the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor, and the saddle Hessian.

title: Structured Confidence Perturbation via Fisher Geometry for Adversarial Training
abstract: Adversarial training is often plagued by "pseudo-attacks", perturbations that significantly increase the loss value but fail to truly alter the model's confidence structure. To address this, we propose two complementary approaches to directly attack and defend against confidence structure deformation. First, building upon the traditional loss maximization perspective, we introduce a hybrid objective that integrates cross-entropy and KL divergence, encouraging adversarial examples to simultaneously disrupt prediction accuracy and distribution consistency. Second, we geometrically reconstruct adversarial training by generating perturbations that maximize the distribution distance on the confidence manifold. Theoretical analysis shows that the optimal perturbation direction aligns with the principal eigenvectors of the Fisher information matrix. We also propose an efficient algorithm to avoid high-dimensional matrix computations. Experiments on multiple datasets and model architectures demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods in adversarial robustness and robust transferability, particularly excelling in structural perturbations within high-confidence regions.

title: Lipschitz-Controlled Flow Matching for Robust Image Restoration
abstract: Flow-matching models can produce high-quality image restorations, but their learned dynamics may amplify small input perturbations and make reconstructions unstable. We also use adversarial finite-radius gain regularization at sampled interpolation states to penalize excessive sensitivity to the state and, for conditional sampling, the observation. We test both formulations on blind face restoration, measuring adversarial robustness and the perceptual quality of the reconstructions. LipsFlower reduces perturbation amplification while keeping restoration quality competitive with the evaluated baselines. These results suggest that Lipschitz-aware flow matching can improve the stability of generative image restoration.

title: POEM: Output-Relative Block-Sparse Attention for Long-Context Prefilling
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

title: AI Alignment Is Neither Solvable nor Sufficient
abstract: Humans and AI systems increasingly act within the same social and economic environments. Alignment, the goal of ensuring that AI systems act in accordance with human values, is widely regarded as a central challenge for ensuring that AI benefits society while avoiding harm. We argue that this endeavor is misguided. First, alignment is not well defined, as it presumes a sufficiently stable and identifiable set of human intentions or values. Second, where a concrete notion of alignment can be specified, it is not solvable. Third, where alignment appears solvable, solving it would not necessarily mitigate the negative consequences of AI. A key reason is that alignment is typically framed as a property of individual AI systems, while the resulting hybrid societies of humans and machines are complex systems shaped by interactions and feedback loops. Emergent risks, and not only those posed by individual misaligned systems, are therefore likely to become a major source of harm. We conclude that AI safety is an ongoing challenge and not a problem that can be solved once and for all by verifying a particular model property.

title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
abstract: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.

title: Can the Confidence and Decisions of System 1 Models Be Trusted? An Explainability and Perturbation Audit of Jev-Style Decision Models
abstract: "System 1" decision models (pioneered by TypeSafe AI's Jev) replace autoregressive text generation with a single forward pass returning typed probability distributions over declared schemas (Choice, Score, Noul). While deployed for low-latency routing and automated triage, their statistical calibration and post-hoc explainability remain uncharacterized. We introduce an open, deterministic audit benchmark evaluating System 1 decision models across calibration under label-preserving perturbations, cross-question interference, and post-hoc attribution faithfulness. Evaluating five open-weight models (0.8B to 27B) alongside generative System 2 baselines -- both single-token logprob scoring and structured JSON/CoT decoding -- across NLI (e-SNLI), adversarial syntactic shortcuts (HANS), synthetic clinical triage (N=900), prompt injection defense (Tensor Trust, N=250), and an 86-case logic-gate trigger suite yields five findings: (1) provider confidence is an exact closed-form dispersion transform (1 - H(p)/ln K on sub-10B models; normalized margin on Clef-27B) rather than empirical accuracy; (2) bundling multiple questions in one request induces directional cross-question interference (11.7% to 22.4% binary flips on Tev1-0.8B, vs. 0.1% to 0.2% on Tev1-4B); (3) System 1 models with >= 4B parameters are faster and better calibrated under syntactic shifts (ECE_w = 0.030 to 0.087) than logprob (0.144) and JSON (0.378) baselines; (4) for prompt-injection defense (N=250), >= 4B models achieve 0.988 to 0.998 AUROC with up to 95.2% recall and 0.0% false alarms at 48 to 60 ms; and (5) single-pass inference makes 512-coalition XAI interactive (1.3 to 3.2 s/input), while KernelSHAP with a logit link (S1-SHAP) mitigates softmax saturation on disjunctive OR gates (89.3% to 100.0% gate recovery vs. 57.1% to 82.1% in prob space; p_adj = 0.004).

title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
abstract: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and never with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.

title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
abstract: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection. To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests. We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.

title: AnyBreak: Towards Jailbreaking Any T2I Model for Any Concept
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in image generation and editing, yet this progress has also introduced significant security risks. Prior work has shown that adversarial prompt can induce the generation of Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content, including pornographic, violent, and graphic imagery. However, such attacks are typically mitigated by prompt filters and often rely on white-box assumptions. In this paper, we propose AnyBreak, a novel jailbreak framework that constructs adversarial images via multi-scale progressive semantic alignment. During the generation process, these adversarial images steer the generation trajectory in latent space towards unsafe data manifolds, enabling cross-modal transfer of malicious concepts from the text modality to the image modality. AnyBreak operates using only clean textual prompts and adversarial images at inference time, and can jailbreak any T2I models towards any malicious concepts in a fully black-box setting. We further introduce AnyBreak-V, an enhanced variant that incorporates a compensation term to bypass post-hoc safety checkers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AnyBreak achieves high attack success rates while preserving visual fidelity and semantic consistency with the input prompts under black-box and clean-text constraints. Our findings reveal that existing T2I defense leave critical cross-modal attack surfaces insufficiently addressed. The code is available at https://github.com/luqi-glory/AnyBreak.

title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
abstract: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured. To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations. Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
abstract: Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. As of Fall 2026, human red-teaming may be nearing saturation, especially on the Gemini family of models. In this work, we argue that despite this apparent plateau, prompt injection attacks are still possible and continued effort into prompt injection defense is needed. We design a new synthetic evaluation dataset which uses random non-malicious actions as adversarial goals. Such dataset design helps us to evaluate prompt injection robustness as a model ability to respect instruction hierarchy, and disentangle this ability from model knowledge of security practices. We show that an agentic attacker of increased capabilities can reliably trick model to follow instructions in tool output in our evaluation, even for models previously considered robust on public prompt injection benchmarks such as GraySwan Arena. This shows that current frontier defenses may require proactive, automated red-teaming to remain resilient to increasingly capable adversaries.

title: Direct Trajectory Optimization for Inference-Time Alignment of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
abstract: Alignment of text-to-image diffusion models with reward functions is a key challenge in controllable generation. Existing approaches typically rely on optimizing model inputs or fine-tuning denoising networks, which requires computationally expensive backpropagation through large denoising models. In this work, we propose Direct Trajectory Optimization (DTO), a training-free framework that performs alignment by directly optimizing the sampling trajectory of diffusion models. Specifically, DTO treats intermediate denoising scores and sampled noise as the optimization variables, eliminating the need for gradients through the denoising network. To mitigate the out-of-distribution problem, we introduce Reward-Optimized Score Guidance, which interpolates between the optimized scores and the pretrained model predictions to stabilize sampling, while providing a provable theoretical guarantee of reward improvement under constrained distributions. Empirically, DTO improves alignment performance across three diffusion models on two benchmarks, outperforming existing inference-time alignment methods while maintaining high efficiency. These results suggest that trajectory-level optimization is a promising direction for efficient and effective diffusion model alignment.

title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents act on instructions embedded in the data they read, so prompt injection is a structural rather than a prompt-wording problem. We compare in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting, LLM detectors) with deterministic enforcement outside the model (four reference monitors of increasing strength), human approval and taint tracking, judged by one effect-based oracle independent of every defence in an executable environment of 13 tasks and 12 tools, with argument-fuzzing attackers and severity-weighted harm. In an evaluation with real open-weights models (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B; 156 attack episodes per defence and model), the models proposed the attacker's call in 64% and 84% of attack episodes behind the task-bound monitor, which admitted 1.3% and 7.7%; guardrail effects depended on the model (a prompt guardrail moved obedience from 67% to 65% and from 86% to 55%, spotlighting plus a detector to 12% and 0%) against static attacks. Simulation with an assumed model covers what no real run did: under the assumed erosion law a persistent adaptive attacker or a compromised model drives every guardrail stack to 100.0% attack success, whereas the task-bound monitor holds severe actions at 0.0%; its residual (harm 0.69/10) falls by 62% under taint-triggered human review, and a human layer without a deterministic monitor fails against approval spamming unless each episode has a deterministic approval budget. Implementation quality matters: a naive monitor admits 18 of 33 effective attack variants, a hardened one 6 and a capability-bound one 1. The real-model evidence is limited to two open-weights models and static attacks, the human-approval and taint results are simulation-only, and the larger model's detector stack contradicts the assumed erosion law. Code, data, a two-rater oracle audit and a notebook for repeating the real-model evaluation are provided.

title: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents
abstract: An LLM agent that reads untrusted content, such as an email or a web page, may follow instructions hidden in it. Noninterference is too strong for such agents, since a useful agent lets untrusted content influence what it does and may disclose the user's data by design, and declassification needs a release policy written for each task. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. An agent is relatively secure if every leak it has is a leak the reference already has. Our framework, PlanTERS, instantiates relative security, a notion from speculative execution, with a small agent language in which the attacker chooses how the model follows instructions, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe. A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for every model behaviour in which each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance; with a fairness condition, this extends to possibly infinite runs. We prove or refute relative security for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.
